claims.text: The modified alloy is an equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is single-phase and in a solidified solid-solution state.
Removing Co lowers the local stacking-fault energy in the FeNiCrMn alloy.
The proposed stacking-fault-energy reduction is especially associated with the [110] crystallographic direction.
Lower local stacking-fault energy enables easier dislocation nucleation.
Lower local stacking-fault energy enhances slip activity at elevated temperatures and high strain rates.
The Co-removal-induced change in dislocation activation accounts for the retained strength–ductility balance under dynamic loading.
Removing Co alters the alloy's electronic environment.
Removing Co alters the alloy's lattice environment.
The altered electronic and lattice environment reduces the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation on stacking-fault-energy-sensitive slip systems.
Easier slip activation increases dislocation density under dynamic conditions.
At elevated temperature and high strain rate, [110]-loaded Co-free FeNiCrMn will have a lower dislocation nucleation stress than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested identically.
At elevated temperature and high strain rate, [110]-loaded Co-free FeNiCrMn will have a higher mobile-dislocation density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested identically.
The Co-free alloy's stress–strain curve will show lower nucleation stress accompanied by greater ductility relative to the Co-containing baseline.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has higher stacking-fault energy than the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy under identical conditions.
The higher stacking-fault energy of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi produces higher dislocation activation stresses.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys in the solid-solution state under simulated uniaxial tension within the tested temperature and strain-rate ranges.
A lack of a statistically significant nucleation-stress decrease and dislocation-density increase in Co-free FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi would falsify the hypothesis.
